I agree with the above observations that it should be relatively simple to send either a manned or unmanned expedition to the Summit. But what I really wanted to comment on is the use of [DATA EXPUNGED] in the document rather than [REDACTED] or black bars. I know, yeah it means the same thing out-of-universe … But in-universe, they would never permanently delete information without a damn good reason for it, such as when an AI construct is used to observe a cognitohazard and describe it, and then later must delete part of the description because even the words on the screen turn out to be enough to nuke peoples' brains. Or another example of expungement would be if the O-5 Council receives a top-secret report and they decide that for whatever reason nobody who doesn't already know about it should ever learn about it. Or an example that is used in the real world is certain criminal activities that can be expunged from the record, either in the case of a minor offense that has already been paid for, or in the case of potentially major offenses that are expunged in exchange for witness testimony or exposition of another party's even greater offenses.

I know it probably sounds like a minor thing to be a stickler about, but even if the original author isn't around to care anymore it may be helpful to someone else who might want to use the correct terminology in their own stuff.

It's commonly accepted that the foundation has access to more advanced technology than the general public, I believe. Docking in orbit is fairly simple, not to mention that there have been successful landings of probes on speeding comets. How come there has been no such effort by the foundation?
Barring something as costly as that, why not just send a drone capable of climbing the rope up to the summit?
Though I find the object itself very interesting, it's somewhat ruined for me by how halfhearted the attempts to investigate have been, considering what the foundation has access too. It honestly feels kinda like the writer was just trying to avoid having to come up with what the summit is, and that's a -1 from me.

item.title: Re:
item.content:encoded:
Indeed. 39 km isn't even out of Earth's atmosphere to any appreciable degree, though it's far enough up that you couldn't breathe up there.

I think calling the summit object a "satellite" is probably just too misleading and the changes that would be necessary to make it into a satellite are too great. For example, if it really was geostationary it'd be directly above the equator, so the rope would rise at an angle of somewhere between approximately 30 and 40 degrees (depending on where in Tibet the mountain is) from vertical. Furthermore, there'd be satellite collisions with it - this is one of the major risks faced by space elevator designs in real life.

I think it's best to just describe the summit object as an "object" of some sort. It's no more a satellite than a tethered balloon would be.
